headline: Race Point Rip Holds the Bass Through the Ebb, Cod Nosing Onto Peaked Hill Bars
subhead: Bluefish are chewing peanut bunker off Sandy Neck while the first cod of the season start showing on the deeper humps north of Race Point.
body_markdown:
The fleet out of P-town has been working the same rhythm for about ten days now, and it's held up better than most late-August weeks do. Race Point continues to be the anchor of the bite — the rip off the Point still has enough current and bait pushing through it on the tide changes to keep stripers stacked on the structure, and that's been the case whether the wind has cooperated or not. We flagged this last week — said the early tide stages would remain the best bet through the short-term stretch — and that's exactly how it's played out. First two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood at Race Point have outproduced the middle of either tide almost every day this week.

Water's still holding summer warmth in the Bay, but the nights are getting a jump on things. You can feel it on the ride out in the morning — there's a little more bite to the air, and that's the signal that starts pulling bait around and eventually pulls the bass and the first cod onto the deeper structure. Wind has been mostly out of the southwest, light to moderate, which keeps the west side of the Bay fishable most mornings before it builds into the afternoon. Moon's working toward full over the next several days, and that added tidal push should start concentrating bait tighter on the rips and shoals rather than letting it spread out over open water — that's usually when the better-grade fish show up in numbers rather than just a few here and there.

Striper fishing on the rip has been solid, not spectacular. Fish are running mostly mid-20s to mid-30-inch class, with enough better fish mixed in — high 30s, occasional low 40s — to keep boats making repeat drifts. The pattern that's working is live mackerel under a balloon or slow-trolled on a fishfinder rig, drifted right through the seam where the rip stands up against the current, usually 20 to 35 feet of water depending on where the bait's holding that day. Bucktails in the 2 to 3-ounce range, white or chartreuse, dropped to the bottom and worked with a slow lift-and-drop through the same water, have also been taking fish, particularly on the last of the ebb when the current starts to ease and the bass tuck tighter to bottom. Peaked Hill Bars has been more hit or miss — good when the swell's down and the bait's sitting on the bar, dead when there's any groundswell running, which has been the case a few days this week.

Bluefish have been the more dependable player right now, and that tracks with what we expected — bluefish activity following bait density, and the peanut bunker showing up thick along Sandy Neck has brought the blues right in tight to the beach. Surfcasters working the flats off Sandy Neck at first light have had steady action on metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks — worked fast through the bait schools as they get pushed up against the beach on the last of the incoming tide. Boat guys working just outside the bar have done well with small umbrella rigs and Ava jigs in the same window. Sizes have been average, two to four pounds, with some better fish mixed in when the bait balls get pushed tighter.

Fluke are in that typical late-summer holding pattern — still catchable, but you have to work for it. Billingsgate has been giving up keeper-class fish on the deeper edges of the shoal, and Barnstable Harbor's channel has produced some decent fluke on the last of the ebb when the water's draining hard off the flats. Gulp in white or pink, three to four inches, on a light bucktail or a simple fluke rig with a strip of squid, worked slow along the channel edges in 15 to 25 feet, has been the go-to. Nothing wide open, but enough to make an afternoon worthwhile if you're patient and willing to move around.

Cod are the story to watch heading into September. A handful of boats working the deeper structure north of Race Point and along the edges toward Peaked Hill have started picking up a few fish on diamond jigs and clam bait, nothing consistent yet, but that's the usual pattern this time of year — as the surface layer cools and mixes down, cod start nosing back onto the humps and wrecks they abandoned back in June. Worth keeping an eye on over the next couple weeks as nights keep shortening.

Looking ahead, the moon building toward full should tighten up bait on the rips and give the striper bite at Race Point a real chance to improve rather than just hold steady. If the wind stays out of the southwest and doesn't build too hard, the early tide stages there remain the play — first light on the ebb, or the top of the flood before the crowds show up for the holiday weekend. Sandy Neck should keep producing blues as long as that peanut bunker stays put, and Billingsgate's still worth a drift for fluke if you're not married to the idea of a bent rod every cast. Keep a rod rigged for cod if you're running north past the Point — the early signs are there, even if the numbers aren't yet.
